Destroyed crops bring every household into mourning

The locusts strike one group after another. Drinkers lose their wine (verse 5), and farmers lose their harvest (verse 11). Verse 9 says the offerings in God’s house have stopped. With no grain or wine there is nothing to bring. So the disaster reaches worship as well as food. Verse 14 treats it as a summons. Everyone must gather, fast, and cry to the LORD.
An alarm becomes a call to gather and return

Tearing one’s clothes was a visible sign of grief. Verse 13 asks for the inward form of it. Its ground is God’s character, quoted from Exodus 34:6. Verse 14 adds “Who knows?” The people may hope, and they may not presume. Verse 16 calls everyone, even infants and a bride and groom. Peter quotes verses 28–32 in Acts 2:16–21.
Judgment answers the sale and scattering of people

The charge in verse 3 is the sale of children. A boy was traded for a night with a prostitute. A girl was sold for the price of a drink. The cheapness of the price shows how little their lives counted. Verses 6–8 add that Judah’s children were sold to distant peoples. The judgment answers in kind. Verse 10 reverses the hope of Isaiah 2:4, and plows become swords.
